# The Caenorhabditis elegans protein SAS-5 forms large oligomeric assemblies critical for centriole formation ## Authors - Kacper B Rogala1 - Nicola J Dynes3 - Georgios N Hatzopoulos1 - Jun Yan4 - Sheng Kai Pong3 - Carol V Robinson4 - Charlotte M Deane2 - Pierre Gönczy3 † - Ioannis Vakonakis1 † ### Affiliations 1. Department of Biochemistry University of Oxford Oxford United Kingdom 2. Department of Statistics University of Oxford Oxford United Kingdom 3. Swiss Institute for Experimental Cancer Research, School of Life Sciences Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne Switzerland 4. Department of Chemistry University of Oxford Oxford United Kingdom † Corresponding author ## Abstract Centrioles are microtubule-based organelles crucial for cell division, sensing and motility. In Caenorhabditis elegans, the onset of centriole formation requires notably the proteins SAS-5 and SAS-6, which have functional equivalents across eukaryotic evolution. Whereas the molecular architecture of SAS-6 and its role in initiating centriole formation are well understood, the mechanisms by which SAS-5 and its relatives function is unclear. Here, we combine biophysical and structural analysis to uncover the architecture of SAS-5 and examine its functional implications in vivo. Our work reveals that two distinct self-associating domains are necessary to form higher-order oligomers of SAS-5: a trimeric coiled coil and a novel globular dimeric Implico domain. Disruption of either domain leads to centriole duplication failure in worm embryos, indicating that large SAS-5 assemblies are necessary for function in vivo. ## Introduction Most eukaryotes harbor microtubule-based cylindrical organelles called centrioles that exhibit a striking ninefold radial symmetry, and which are crucial for a wide range of cellular functions (reviewed in Gönczy, 2012; Agircan et al., 2014). In resting cells, centrioles are usually found near the plasma membrane where they organize the formation of flagella and cilia, whereas in proliferating cells centrioles typically reside adjacent to the nucleus, where they recruit pericentriolar material to form the centrosome, the major microtubule organizing center of animal cells. Centrosomes play a major role in directing cellular architecture during interphase and bipolar spindle assembly during mitosis. Centriole numbers are tightly regulated, with centriole duplication occurring only once per cell cycle, in concert with replication of the genetic material (reviewed in Firat-Karalar and Stearns, 2014). Abnormalities in centriole formation can impair cell signaling and motility owing to defective cilia or flagella, as well as cause spindle positioning defects and genome instability due to aberrations in centrosome numbers and/or sizes. Thus, it is not surprising that centriolar defects are at the root of multiple medical conditions, including primary microcephaly, male sterility and possibly cancer (reviewed in Nigg and Raff, 2009; Arquint et al., 2014; Chavali et al., 2014; Godinho and Pellman, 2014; and Nachury, 2014). Five proteins required for centriole assembly were originally identified in Caenorhabditis elegans through genetic analysis and functional genomics (reviewed in Gönczy, 2012); these include the recruiting factor SPD-2 (Kemp et al., 2004; Pelletier et al., 2004), the kinase ZYG-1 (O'connell et al., 2001), and the coiled-coil domain containing proteins SAS-5, SAS-6 and SAS-4 (Kirkham et al., 2003; Leidel and Gönczy, 2003; Dammermann et al., 2004; Delattre et al., 2004; Leidel et al., 2005). Following localization of these five proteins to the site of new centriole formation, recruitment of microtubules completes the assembly process, giving rise to a ninefold- symmetric centriole ∼100 nm in diameter (Pelletier et al., 2006). Functionally equivalent proteins have now been identified throughout eukaryotes (Carvalho-Santos et al., 2010; Hodges et al., 2010), indicating an evolutionary shared assembly pathway for centriole formation. Whereas SAS-6 is critical for establishing the ninefold radial symmetry of centrioles (reviewed in Gönczy, 2012; and Hirono, 2014), the underlying structural mechanism differs between C. elegans and other species. Crystallographic and/or electron microscopic analysis supports the view that recombinant SAS-6 proteins from Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, Danio rerio and Leishmania major form ninefold-symmetric rings (Kitagawa et al., 2011b; Van Breugel et al., 2011; Van Breugel et al., 2014). Such SAS-6 rings are thought to dictate the ninefold- symmetrical assembly of the entire centriole. In contrast, similar analysis of C. elegans SAS-6 suggests formation of a spiral oligomer with 4.5-fold symmetry per turn, thus generating ninefold symmetry upon two turns of the spiral (Hilbert et al., 2013). C. elegans SAS-6 physically interacts with SAS-5 (Leidel et al., 2005; Qiao et al., 2012; Hilbert et al., 2013; Lettman et al., 2013), a protein that shuttles rapidly between the cytoplasm and centrioles throughout the cell cycle (Delattre et al., 2004). The presence of SAS-6 and SAS-5 at centrioles is essential for formation of the central tube, a cylindrical structure at the core of the emerging centriole (Pelletier et al., 2006). Depletion of SAS-5 (Dammermann et al., 2004; Delattre et al., 2004) or SAS-5 mutants that are unable to bind SAS-6 (Delattre et al., 2004; Qiao et al., 2012; Lettman et al., 2013) prevent central tube formation, and therefore centriole assembly. Although SAS-5 has been proposed to assist SAS-6 organization (Qiao et al., 2012; Lettman et al., 2013), the mechanisms by which this may be achieved are not known, in part because the architecture of SAS-5 has not yet been resolved. Here, we employ biophysical methods and X-ray crystallography, together with functional assays in C. elegans embryos, to demonstrate that large assemblies of SAS-5 are necessary for centriole formation. Our results lead us to propose a working model in which SAS-5 oligomers may assist function by providing a multivalent framework for the assembly of C. elegans SAS-6 oligomers. ## Results ### SAS-5 features two independently folded domains Previous attempts at recombinant expression of full-length C. elegans SAS-5 (SAS-5FL, amino acids 1–404, Figure 1A) yielded insoluble or marginally soluble material (Qiao et al., 2012; Lettman et al., 2013). To tackle this problem, we constructed a bacterial expression vector system harboring 13 different solubility-tags, which allowed us to obtain soluble SAS-5FL fused to MsyB (Zou et al., 2008) in quantities sufficient for biophysical analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which shows all recombinant proteins in this study). Characterization of such purified SAS-5FL using circular dichroism (CD) revealed the presence of protein aggregates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), a conclusion also supported by size-exclusion chromatography multi-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) and negative-stain electron microscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D). We sought to locate the motif in SAS-5 that causes aggregation by expressing a series of MsyB-tagged C-terminal truncation constructs, and observed a significant increase in solubility when comparing a construct encompassing residues 2–279 with one containing residues 2–296 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3). Secondary structure prediction suggested a β-strand between residues 282 and 295 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). Excising this region from untagged SAS-5FL (SAS-5Δ282–295) or replacing it with a Gly-Ser-Ala-rich flexible linker of equal length (SAS-5FLEX) resulted in proteins with CD spectra characteristic of mainly α-helical proteins (Figure 1B). Interestingly, thermal unfolding of the soluble SAS-5Δ282–295 and SAS-5FLEX variants showed a two-step cooperative melting process, thus revealing the presence of two independently folded domains (Figure 1C). Sequence-based prediction suggested the presence of a coiled coil spanning residues 125–180, as well as of three tightly-spaced α-helices (residues 210–265); these two elements are separated from each other by a presumed disordered linker of ∼30 residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). We expressed both the coiled coil (SAS-5CC) and the predicted helical region (SAS-5Imp for Implico, see below) and performed CD analysis. SAS-5CC displayed a double-minimum spectrum (Figure 1D) characteristic of α-helical coiled coils, and exhibited moderate thermal stability in isolation (apparent melting transition temperature, Tm ∼ 37°C, Figure 1E). In contrast, CD of SAS-5Imp revealed a very stable (Tm ∼ 72°C) α-helical domain (Figure 1D,E). A SAS-5 construct that combined both the coiled coil and the α-helical domain (SAS-5125–265, residues 125–265) showed CD spectra and a two-step thermal unfolding profile highly similar to that of SAS-5Δ282–295 and SAS-5FLEX (compare Figure 1F,G with Figure 1B,C). We attribute the first melting transition of SAS-5125–265 (Tm of ∼50°C) to unfolding of the coiled-coil domain and the second (Tm of ∼70°C) to unfolding of the Implico domain. Moreover, CD spectra of isolated SAS-5 N-terminal (residues 2–122) or C-terminal (269–404) fragments showed no persistent secondary structure or cooperative thermal unfolding (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), consistent with similar previous analysis of the SAS-5 N-terminus (Shimanovskaya et al., 2013). Overall, these findings led us to conclude that the segment between residues 125–265 contains two independently folded domains and encompasses all structured elements of SAS-5. ### The SAS-5 coiled coil forms a moderately stable trimer We next set out to determine the X-ray crystallographic structures of the two independently folded domains. Native crystals of SAS-5CC diffracted to 1.8 Å resolution, whilst phases for structure solution were determined by single anomalous dispersion (SAD) using trimethyl lead acetate derivatized crystals (Tables 1, 2). The structure of SAS-5CC suggested a parallel trimeric coiled coil, although this arrangement is distorted by crystal packing that intercalates the ends of successive triple helical bundles (Figure 2A). To correct for these distortions, we performed molecular dynamics (MD) simulations starting from the crystallographic structure of SAS-5CC, which rapidly converged to a trimeric coiled-coil structure (Figure 2B–D). SEC-MALS analysis of a slightly longer coiled-coil construct (SAS-5CC-L, residues 101–206) demonstrated formation of a trimer in solution in a concentration-dependent manner, with apparent Kd of ∼3 μM (Figure 2G,H). Both the crystallographic model and MD simulations show a series of hydrophobic residues (W133, M137, L141, I144, I148, L159, M167 and M171) forming the core of the coiled coil and enabling trimer formation (Figure 2E,F). Interestingly, we found that all these residues are conserved or conservatively substituted in SAS-5 homologs in other Caenorhabditis species, suggesting functional relevance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). To investigate the stability of the coiled-coil domain across nematode evolution, we expressed constructs corresponding to SAS-5CC-L from Caenorhabditis brenneri, Caenorhabditis briggsae, Caenorhabditis remanei, Caenorhabditis sinica and Caenorhabditis tropicalis. In all cases, SEC-MALS analysis showed similar oligomerization properties and apparent affinities as for C. elegans SAS-5CC-L (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). Taken together, these data suggest that the trimeric coiled coil is an evolutionary conserved feature of nematode SAS-5 proteins. **Table 1.** Crystallographic data collection and refinement statistics

We found that this newly recognized domain is highly conserved amongst Caenorhabditis species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Importantly, SEC-MALS experiments revealed that SAS-5Imp forms a stable dimer (Figure 3A). Crystals of SAS-5Imp diffracted to 1.0 Å resolution and experimental phases were determined by SAD from mercury acetate derivatized samples (Table 1). The SAS-5Imp structure revealed a dimer composed of interlocked chains arranged in an antiparallel fashion (Figure 3B). Each chain features three α-helices (A1 to A3 and B1 to B3) that interact in a pairwise manner (A1–B3, A2–B2 and A3–B1). Proline residues at the linkers between helices allow for tight 90° turns (Figure 3C), resulting in a very compact dimer of just ∼4 nm in diameter. The dimer interface (Figure 3D) involves the majority of hydrophobic core residues (I219, I225, A229, L230, I232, I233, L237, F243, I247, V250, L251); thus, breaking the dimer is expected to unfold the SAS-5Imp domain. Given the high thermal stability of SAS-5Imp (Figure 1E), this suggests formation of stable dimers even at very low protein concentrations. Universally conserved residues are indicated by red highlight; conservatively substituted residues are shown in red. ### The molecular architecture of SAS-5 drives the formation of higher-order assemblies Together, the two oligomerization domains of SAS-5 have the potential to drive formation of protein assemblies of higher-order than merely dimers or trimers. We envision that SAS-5 would readily dimerize even at low concentrations via the Implico domain, as oligomerization of this domain is tighter compared to that of the SAS-5 coiled coil. Such SAS-5 dimers could then come together to form higher-order configurations. To test this possibility, we performed SEC-MALS experiments on MsyB-tagged SAS-5FLEX, which revealed concentration-dependent oligomerization of SAS-5 from dimers to an approximately equimolar population of tetramers and hexamers (Figure 4A,B). Analogous results were obtained with a MsyB-tagged SAS-5 construct that lacks the disordered protein C-terminus (SAS-52–265) (Figure 4C,D). Moreover, native mass-spectrometry of SAS-52–265 also supported the presence of higher-order protein assemblies up to hexamers in solution (Figure 4E). Taken together, these data support the notion that the SAS-5 coiled coil promotes the association of protein dimers towards higher-order assemblies. Furthermore, our results are consistent with an earlier SEC-MALS analysis of MBP-tagged SAS-5 constructs of residues 1–260, which showed formation of tetramers at an unspecified protein concentration (Shimanovskaya et al., 2013). ![Figure 4.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/07410/elife-07410-fig4-v2.jpg) **Figure 4.:** (A) Overlay of SEC-MALS chromatograms of MsyB-tagged SAS-5FLEX in multiple concentrations and (B) plot of average molecular weight from SEC-MALS analysis as a function of on-column protein concentration. The apparent Kd and molecular sizes of dimers, tetramers and hexamers are indicated. SAS-5FLEX-MsyB reaches an equimolar hexamer to tetramer ratio at the highest concentration we could assess. Fitting the experimental data under the assumption of ultimate hexamer formation yielded Kd values comparable to those of the SAS-5 coiled coil in isolation (compared B with Figure 2H). (C,D) Similar SEC-MALS analysis of MsyB-tagged SAS-52–265. SAS-52–265-MsyB reaches a 3:1 hexamer to tetramer ratio at the highest concentration point. (E) Native mass-spectrometry electrospray ionization spectrum of a 20 μM sample of SAS-52–265, showing relative abundance of protein species as a function of mass to charge ratio. The charged states and protein oligomeric forms corresponding to specific peaks are indicated. Odd-numbered oligomeric forms (monomers, trimers etc) likely correspond to in-flight breakdown of higher- order protein assemblies. To further probe the architectural model of higher-order SAS-5 assemblies, we proceeded to disrupt each oligomerization interface by engineering charged residues in place of core hydrophobic amino acids. The CD spectra of the resulting SAS-5CC L141E mutant showed significant reduction of α-helical content in the coiled coil and a striking reduction in stability (Tm < 10°C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), whereas that of the SAS-5Imp I247E mutant showed absence of α-helical structure and complete loss of cooperativity upon thermal unfolding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D). We next engineered the same substitutions in the SAS-52–265 construct to selectively disrupt each oligomerization interface whilst leaving the other intact. We found that the thermal unfolding profile of a SAS-52–265 L141E mutant showed a reduction in stability of the coiled coil by approximately 25°C, whereas stability of the Implico domain was not affected (Figure 5A,B). Substituting an additional core hydrophobic residue of the coiled coil (SAS-52–265 L141E/M167E) effectively abrogated coiled coil formation, again with no effect on the Implico domain (Figure 5A,B). We found that whereas GFP-SAS-5 is enriched at centrioles (Figure 6F,I and Delattre et al., 2004), as was also observed by live imaging, the situation differed for both oligomerization interface mutants. In the case of GFP-SAS-5 L141E, only ∼30% of centrosomes exhibited a clear GFP focus, with the remaining centrosomes exhibiting either no GFP focus, or only a weak focus (Figure 6G,I). In the case of GFP-SAS-5 I247E, the vast majority of embryos exhibited no detectable GFP focus at centrioles (Figure 6H,I). We conclude that SAS-5 oligomerization is important for centriole localization, with the Implico domain playing a particularly critical role in this respect. Moreover, the presence of GFP-SAS-5 L141E at centrioles in one third of embryos, combined with the fact that this mutant completely failed to rescue the phenotype, raises the possibility that formation of higher-order SAS-5 assemblies is essential for function even if centriolar localization has been achieved. ## Discussion C. elegans SAS-5 lies at the heart of centriole duplication, given that it associates with SAS-6 (Leidel et al., 2005; Qiao et al., 2012; Hilbert et al., 2013; Lettman et al., 2013), a critical structural component for the establishment of the ninefold symmetry of centrioles (Kitagawa et al., 2011b; Van Breugel et al., 2011; Hilbert et al., 2013; Van Breugel et al., 2014), and it is required for SAS-6 centriolar localization. Previous biophysical analysis of the SAS-5/SAS-6 interaction was performed using relatively short C-terminal SAS-5 peptides (Qiao et al., 2012; Hilbert et al., 2013), as full-length SAS-5 proved difficult to purify. Our results show that SAS-5 aggregates in vitro due to a ∼20 amino acid segment that may form a β-strand (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4); this site is outside the SAS-5 region implicated in SAS-6 binding (Qiao et al., 2012; Hilbert et al., 2013; Lettman et al., 2013). Although we cannot exclude the possibility that SAS-5 multimerization through this predicted β-strand is physiologically relevant, we do not favor such interpretation. The aggregates formed by full-length SAS-5, as visualized by EM, are proportional in size to C. elegans centrioles even at very low protein concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D). Thus, if present in vivo, the large size of such aggregates would leave little, if any, space for other centriolar components, including SAS-6, SAS-4 and microtubules. Rather, we postulate that in vivo SAS-5 forms a complex with a yet unidentified partner using the ∼20 amino acid segment identified here, and that this complex protects SAS-5 from aggregation in the cell. It is intriguing to speculate whether Protein Phosphatase 2A, which binds SAS-5 in vivo and controls SAS-5 levels (Song et al., 2011; Kitagawa et al., 2011a), may interact with SAS-5 in this region. Structural and biophysical analysis suggests that SAS-5 can form tight dimers through its Implico domain, a novel dimerization interface with no known homologs outside SAS-5 proteins (Figure 3). These dimers cannot be disrupted even when diluting the protein to concentrations as low as 20 nM (Figure 4A–D). By comparison, the dimer mediated by the SAS-6 coiled coil is approximately 50-times weaker (Kitagawa et al., 2011b), yet the human orthologue HsSAS-6 readily forms dimers in cells (Keller et al., 2014). By extension, it appears reasonable to assume that SAS-5 forms dimers in the cytoplasm of C. elegans embryos. Such dimers would associate with SAS-6 (Delattre et al., 2004; Qiao et al., 2012; Hilbert et al., 2013; Lettman et al., 2013) and possibly SAS-4 (Cottee et al., 2013; Hatzopoulos et al., 2013), given the moderate interaction strengths of these associations. Our work shows that formation of these tight SAS-5 dimers through the Implico domain is necessary for SAS-5 localization to centrioles (Figure 6H,I). This suggests that the localization mechanism either recognizes the Implico domain itself, or depends on a protein association that needs two copies of a distinct SAS-5 epitope, and hence the SAS-5 dimer. Multivalent protein interactions increase the apparent strength (avidity) of association, and are common in biology (Mammen et al., 1998). It is possible that the interaction of SAS-5 with SAS-6, known to be necessary for localization of both proteins to centrioles (Delattre et al., 2004; Qiao et al., 2012; Lettman et al., 2013), benefits from such an avidity effect. It will be interesting to determine whether the L141E and I247E SAS-5 mutants prevent SAS-6 recruitment to the nascent centriole assembly site or rather prevent SAS-6 from being organized properly thereafter. In either case, this would likely hinder downstream recruitment of SAS-4, and therefore centriole formation (Dammermann et al., 2004; Delattre et al., 2004; Qiao et al., 2012; Lettman et al., 2013). SAS-5 concentrates at centrioles, as illustrated by well-defined GFP foci of this protein (Figure 6F,I), and we propose that SAS-5 dimers associate further to form higher-order assemblies there. Our SEC-MALS results show that SAS-5 forms tetramers already at 1 μM concentration and a mixture of tetramers and hexamers at 10 μM (Figure 4B). Although the SAS-5 architecture, with two independent oligomerization interfaces, could theoretically sustain the formation of open-ended protein chains or networks, we believe it is more likely that higher-order SAS-5 assemblies cap at a hexameric size. Such hexamers, formed through the sequential association of three SAS-5 dimers (Figure 7), should be both kinetically and entropically favored compared to open-ended SAS-5 chains. Hexamer breakdown would require simultaneous disruption of two SAS-5 coiled coils, a rarer event compared to the disruption of a single coiled coil in an open-ended SAS-5 oligomer. Further, in the sequential assembly model of Figure 7, once the first coiled-coil sequence of a SAS-5 dimer has associated into a folded coiled-coil structure, the degrees of freedom of the second SAS-5 coiled-coil sequence would be reduced, and thus its association into the second folded coiled-coil structure would become entropically favored. ![Figure 7.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/07410/elife-07410-fig7-v2.jpg) **Figure 7.:** Schematic representation of SAS-5 oligomerization, showing the coiled-coil and Implico domains, without the disordered N- and C-termini of this protein. Tight dimers of SAS-5, mediated by the Implico domain, could come together through the coiled coil to form, first, a tetramer and ultimately a hexamer in a concentration-dependent manner. This oligomerisation model does not take into account protein aggregation mediated by the predicted β-strand at the SAS-5 C-terminus. Disruption of these SAS-5 coiled-coil assemblies by amino acid substitutions (L141E) weakens localization to centrioles (Figure 6G,I), possibly by impacting the SAS-6 avidity mechanism postulated above. Intriguingly, our data suggest that formation of higher-order SAS-5 assemblies is necessary for function beyond localization, since the GFP-SAS-5 L141E mutant does not rescue centriole duplication upon depletion of endogenous SAS-5, even though it localizes to centrioles in ∼1/3 of embryos (Figure 6D,G,I). Although some GFP-SAS-5 L141E may be provided from centrioles contributed by the sperm where endogenous SAS-5 is present, we anticipate that any paternal SAS-5 will rapidly exchange with the much larger maternal protein pool (Delattre et al., 2004). Thus, we expect that GFP-SAS-5 L141E visualized at centrioles (Figure 6G,I) is the maternal protein localized there. The suggestion that higher-order SAS-5 assemblies may be needed for a function other than localization would imply that this protein is not a simple transporter of SAS-6, but that it acts in an additional, more structural, capacity, as has been suggested elsewhere (Qiao et al., 2012; Lettman et al., 2013). However, FRAP experiments show rapid shuttling of SAS-5 between centrioles and the cytoplasm (Delattre et al., 2004), which seemingly conflicts with such a postulated structural role. How can these observations be reconciled? We speculate that there may exist two different and non-exclusive mechanisms by which large SAS-5 assemblies could assist SAS-6 organization; firstly by providing multivalent SAS-6 attachment sites, and secondly by providing a structural framework. Such SAS-5 assemblies may be transiently located at the site of centriole assembly or, alternatively, could correspond to only a small fraction of total SAS-5, which would have thus gone undetected in FRAP experiments (Delattre et al., 2004). SAS-5 assemblies could bind multiple SAS-6 dimers and bring them together in a confined space (Figure 8). ZYG-1, which interacts with SAS-6 independently of SAS-5 and is also located at the duplication site (Lettman et al., 2013), may provide additional enhancement of local SAS-6 concentration. As the interaction affinity for the assembly of SAS-6 oligomers is weak (Kd ∼ 100 μM, [Kitagawa et al., 2011b]) this increase in local SAS-6 concentration may provide a trigger for SAS-6 oligomerisation. Furthermore, if SAS-5 forms defined hexamers as argued above, these hexamers could recruit up to six SAS-6 dimers (Qiao et al., 2012; Hilbert et al., 2013) at the initiation site of SAS-6 oligomerisation. This number of SAS-6 moieties would be sufficient for just over one turn of the proposed SAS-6 spiral (Hilbert et al., 2013), but not for a SAS-6 ring (Kitagawa et al., 2011b; Van Breugel et al., 2011; Van Breugel et al., 2014). Thus, a hexameric SAS-5 architecture would provide an initial structural guide for the configuration of the SAS-6 oligomer. This would be lost in SAS-5 mutants that disrupt its architecture or its interaction with SAS-6 (Delattre et al., 2004; Qiao et al., 2012; Lettman et al., 2013), therefore explaining the absence of centriole formation. ![Figure 8.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/07410/elife-07410-fig8-v2.jpg) **Figure 8.:** (A) SAS-5 forms tight dimers in the cytoplasm, and it may also associate with SAS-6 dimers depending on the relative levels of each protein. (B) SAS-5 localizes at the centriole, where it forms higher-order assemblies. These assemblies bring together multiple SAS-6 dimers in close proximity to one another, thereby increasing the local SAS-6 concentration. Thus, SAS-5 assemblies create a seeding point from which the SAS-6 oligomer forms (C); the first step in creating the C. elegans central tube. Our model is conceptually similar to that proposed, albeit in the absence of structural data, for the vertebrate analogue of SAS-5, STIL (Ohta et al., 2014), and underlies the possible functional similarities between these two proteins. Although the oligomeric status of STIL has not been resolved yet, that of the Drosophila analogue of SAS-5 and STIL, Ana2 (Stevens et al., 2010), suggests the presence of higher-order assemblies possibly formed through interactions with the dynein light chain (Wang et al., 2011; Slevin et al., 2014). However, the specific structural features of SAS-5 are likely restricted to close homologs of this protein, as we were unable to identify sequences homologous to the SAS-5 coiled-coil and Implico domains in either STIL or Ana2. Further, no SAS-5 homolog has been identified in Trichinella spiralis, a nematode that may feature SAS-6 cartwheels, rather than spirals, at its centrioles (Hilbert et al., 2013). Thus, SAS-5 may have evolved in tandem with SAS-6 in order to accommodate the structural divergence of the latter protein and promote spiral formation. Comparison of the SAS-5 structure with those of Ana2 and STIL will be informative in assessing the extent to which the molecular architecture of these proteins is conserved. In summary, we report here a combined structural and functional analysis of SAS-5 architecture, which underlies the role of large SAS-5 assemblies in centriole duplication in C. elegans embryos. We propose that SAS-5 promotes assembly of SAS-6 into oligomers by providing a multivalent structural framework. ### Note added in proof Cottee, Muchalik et al. ## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.07410.029](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.07410.029)

eLife posts the editorial decision letter and author response on a selection of the published articles (subject to the approval of the authors). An edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the substantive concerns or comments; minor concerns are not usually shown. Reviewers have the opportunity to discuss the decision before the letter is sent (see review process). Similarly, the author response typically shows only responses to the major concerns raised by the reviewers.

Thank you for submitting your work entitled “The Caenorhabditis elegans protein SAS-5 forms large oligomeric assemblies critical for centriole formation” for peer review at eLife. Your submission has been favorably evaluated by John Kuriyan (Senior editor) and two reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

In this manuscript, Rogala et al., investigate the structural characteristics of SAS-5, a C. elegans protein that is essential for centriole formation. Using a variety of biochemical techniques, the authors show that SAS-5 oligomerizes via multiple domains and that SAS-5 oligomerization essential for proper centriole duplication in the C. elegans embryo. Furthermore, the authors determined the crystal structures of a central coiled-coil domain and a novel dimerization domain, which the authors term Implico. This study is well done and provides novel insight on the structure and function of a key centriole protein. Furthermore, the identification of a novel dimerization domain will no doubt be of considerable interest to the wider community.

We have a number of questions that we would like you to address, by further discussion in the text.

How could the flexible SAS-5 hexamer that you propose facilitate the formation of a defined SAS-6 spiral and why would oligomerisation stop with a hexamer at all? Further oligomerization could easily be explained if one considers all the other alternative arrangements of the oligomers e.g., the two coiled coil parts (from one Implico domain dimer) joining up to form a parallel dimer with a free valency to take up a third coiled coil helix (linker between Implico domain and coiled coil is long enough for that) or coiled coil helices provided by different SAS-5 dimers coming together from different sides such that one would get chains or meshworks. How do you think that the resulting amorphous and flexible assembly structurally facilitates a defined SAS-6 assembly.

You propose that SAS-5 multimerization is critical for organizing SAS-6 complexes into spirals with 9-fold symmetry (see the last sentence of the Abstract, the last sentence of the Introduction, and the Discussion). Since this hypothesis has not been tested, I feel that this statement is inappropriate for the Abstract and Introduction. More work could be done to see if purified SAS-5 affects SAS-6 assembly in vitro, but I think that is beyond the scope of this paper. However, I think speculation is appropriate for the Discussion section. Furthermore, in the Discussion section the authors should also consider the possibility that the predicted Beta sheet spanning a.a. 282–295 in SAS-5 might be physiologically relevant and promote further multimerization beyond hexamers. The authors cannot dismiss this possibility since they never tested the functionality of SAS-5Δ282-295 in vivo.

The model in Figure 8 is misleading since the authors never tested if SAS-5 oligomerization affects SAS-6 organization. This figure should be removed.

No reference is made to an earlier characterization of SAS-5 structure published by Shimanovskaya et al., 2013 (Worm). The authors should mention this earlier work, why their results are different, and remove the lines in the Discussion section that claim that their study is the first structural and functional analysis of SAS-5 architecture.

The MALS experiments with the coiled coil construct have not been done at higher concentrations, the use of MD analysis to demonstrate trimerisation of the coiled coil is rather weak evidence and some of the MALS runs in Figure 2G are a bit puzzling: The broad black curve gives a flat MW throughout the peak and the tail, while the brown curves that elute at that tail position are less than half that MW. If the assembly goes concentration dependent monomer-dimer-trimer then that behaviour is a bit hard to understand as the black curve should reflect these steps throughout its very broad peak.

It is not always 100% clear whether the solubility tag has been removed or left on.

CD deconvolution into secondary structure percentages tends not to be very accurate in terms of exact numbers and I would consider just mentioning that constructs where found to be mainly helical and so on.

I'm surprised that the authors didn't test if SAS-5 multimerization affects SAS-6 recruitment in vivo. The strong centriole/cell division phenotype seen in the L141E and I247E mutants might be due to the fact that not enough SAS-6 is recruited to the nascent daughter centriole, rather than SAS-6 not being organized properly once delivered there. The authors could use immunofluorescence to test this possibility.

The model in Figure 4 should be revised so that it is clear that the proposed model is for a modified version of SAS-5 that lacks the central predicted Beta sheet (SAS-5FLEX).

claims.source: Characterization of such purified SAS-5FL using circular dichroism (CD) revealed the presence of protein aggregates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), a conclusion also supported by size-exclusion chromatography multi-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) and negative-stain electron microscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from CD, SEC-MALS, and EM.

claims.claim: A predicted β-strand between residues 282 and 295 of SAS-5 drives formation of large protein aggregates.
claims.source: Secondary structure prediction suggested a β-strand between residues 282 and 295 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). Excising this region from untagged SAS-5FL (SAS-5Δ282–295) or replacing it with a Gly-Ser-Ala-rich flexible linker of equal length (SAS-5FLEX) resulted in proteins with CD spectra characteristic of mainly α-helical proteins (Figure 1B). These results suggest that the predicted β-strand between residues 282–295 of SAS-5 drives formation of large protein aggregates.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing that removal or replacement of this region eliminates aggregation.

claims.claim: Thermal unfolding of SAS-5Δ282–295 and SAS-5FLEX variants showed a two-step cooperative melting process, revealing the presence of two independently folded domains.
claims.source: Interestingly, thermal unfolding of the soluble SAS-5Δ282–295 and SAS-5FLEX variants showed a two-step cooperative melting process, thus revealing the presence of two independently folded domains (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from thermal unfolding studies.

claims.claim: SAS-5 contains a coiled coil spanning residues 125–180.
claims.source: Sequence-based prediction suggested the presence of a coiled coil spanning residues 125–180, as well as of three tightly-spaced α-helices (residues 210–265); these two elements are separated from each other by a presumed disordered linker of ∼30 residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence prediction and experimental validation.

claims.claim: SAS-5 contains three tightly-spaced α-helices spanning residues 210–265.
claims.source: Sequence-based prediction suggested the presence of a coiled coil spanning residues 125–180, as well as of three tightly-spaced α-helices (residues 210–265); these two elements are separated from each other by a presumed disordered linker of ∼30 residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence prediction and experimental validation.

claims.claim: The coiled coil and helical region of SAS-5 are separated by a presumed disordered linker of ∼30 residues.
claims.source: Sequence-based prediction suggested the presence of a coiled coil spanning residues 125–180, as well as of three tightly-spaced α-helices (residues 210–265); these two elements are separated from each other by a presumed disordered linker of ∼30 residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence prediction.

claims.claim: SAS-5CC displays a double-minimum CD spectrum characteristic of α-helical coiled coils.
claims.source: We expressed both the coiled coil (SAS-5CC) and the predicted helical region (SAS-5Imp for Implico, see below) and performed CD analysis. SAS-5CC displayed a double-minimum spectrum (Figure 1D) characteristic of α-helical coiled coils, and exhibited moderate thermal stability in isolation (apparent melting transition temperature, Tm ∼ 37°C, Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental CD data.

claims.claim: SAS-5CC exhibits moderate thermal stability with an apparent Tm of ∼37°C.
claims.source: We expressed both the coiled coil (SAS-5CC) and the predicted helical region (SAS-5Imp for Implico, see below) and performed CD analysis. SAS-5CC displayed a double-minimum spectrum (Figure 1D) characteristic of α-helical coiled coils, and exhibited moderate thermal stability in isolation (apparent melting transition temperature, Tm ∼ 37°C, Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental thermal unfolding data.

claims.claim: SAS-5Imp is a very stable α-helical domain with a Tm of ∼72°C.
claims.source: In contrast, CD of SAS-5Imp revealed a very stable (Tm ∼ 72°C) α-helical domain (Figure 1D,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental CD and thermal unfolding data.

claims.claim: A SAS-5 construct combining both the coiled coil and the α-helical domain (SAS-5125–265) shows CD spectra and a two-step thermal unfolding profile highly similar to that of SAS-5Δ282–295 and SAS-5FLEX.
claims.source: A SAS-5 construct that combined both the coiled coil and the α-helical domain (SAS-5125–265, residues 125–265) showed CD spectra and a two-step thermal unfolding profile highly similar to that of SAS-5Δ282–295 and SAS-5FLEX (compare Figure 1F,G with Figure 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental CD and thermal unfolding data.

claims.claim: The first melting transition of SAS-5125–265 (Tm of ∼50°C) corresponds to unfolding of the coiled-coil domain.
claims.source: We attribute the first melting transition of SAS-5125–265 (Tm of ∼50°C) to unfolding of the coiled-coil domain and the second (Tm of ∼70°C) to unfolding of the Implico domain.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the thermal unfolding data and comparison with isolated domains.

claims.claim: The second melting transition of SAS-5125–265 (Tm of ∼70°C) corresponds to unfolding of the Implico domain.
claims.source: We attribute the first melting transition of SAS-5125–265 (Tm of ∼50°C) to unfolding of the coiled-coil domain and the second (Tm of ∼70°C) to unfolding of the Implico domain.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the thermal unfolding data and comparison with isolated domains.

claims.claim: Isolated SAS-5 N-terminal (residues 2–122) and C-terminal (269–404) fragments show no persistent secondary structure or cooperative thermal unfolding.
claims.source: Moreover, CD spectra of isolated SAS-5 N-terminal (residues 2–122) or C-terminal (269–404) fragments showed no persistent secondary structure or cooperative thermal unfolding (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), consistent with similar previous analysis of the SAS-5 N-terminus (Shimanovskaya et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental CD data and a citation to a prior study.

claims.claim: The segment between residues 125–265 contains two independently folded domains and encompasses all structured elements of SAS-5.
claims.source: Overall, these findings led us to conclude that the segment between residues 125–265 contains two independently folded domains and encompasses all structured elements of SAS-5.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Native crystals of SAS-5CC diffracted to 1.8 Å resolution.
claims.source: Native crystals of SAS-5CC diffracted to 1.8 Å resolution, whilst phases for structure solution were determined by single anomalous dispersion (SAD) using trimethyl lead acetate derivatized crystals (Tables 1, 2).
claims.evidence: This is experimental data from X-ray crystallography.

claims.claim: The structure of SAS-5CC suggests a parallel trimeric coiled coil.
claims.source: The structure of SAS-5CC suggested a parallel trimeric coiled coil, although this arrangement is distorted by crystal packing that intercalates the ends of successive triple helical bundles (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data.

claims.claim: Crystal packing distorts the SAS-5CC structure by intercalating the ends of successive triple helical bundles.
claims.source: The structure of SAS-5CC suggested a parallel trimeric coiled coil, although this arrangement is distorted by crystal packing that intercalates the ends of successive triple helical bundles (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the crystallographic structure.

claims.claim: Molecular dynamics simulations of SAS-5CC rapidly converged to a trimeric coiled-coil structure.
claims.source: To correct for these distortions, we performed molecular dynamics (MD) simulations starting from the crystallographic structure of SAS-5CC, which rapidly converged to a trimeric coiled-coil structure (Figure 2B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data.

claims.claim: SEC-MALS analysis of SAS-5CC-L demonstrated formation of a trimer in solution in a concentration-dependent manner, with apparent Kd of ∼3 μM.
claims.source: SEC-MALS analysis of a slightly longer coiled-coil construct (SAS-5CC-L, residues 101–206) demonstrated formation of a trimer in solution in a concentration-dependent manner, with apparent Kd of ∼3 μM (Figure 2G,H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental SEC-MALS data.

claims.claim: A series of hydrophobic residues (W133, M137, L141, I144, I148, L159, M167 and M171) form the core of the SAS-5 coiled coil and enable trimer formation.
claims.source: Both the crystallographic model and MD simulations show a series of hydrophobic residues (W133, M137, L141, I144, I148, L159, M167 and M171) forming the core of the coiled coil and enabling trimer formation (Figure 2E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by crystallographic and MD simulation data.

claims.claim: All hydrophobic core residues of the SAS-5 coiled coil are conserved or conservatively substituted in SAS-5 homologs in other Caenorhabditis species.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that all these residues are conserved or conservatively substituted in SAS-5 homologs in other Caenorhabditis species, suggesting functional relevance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data.

claims.claim: SAS-5 coiled-coil constructs from C. brenneri, C. briggsae, C. remanei, C. sinica and C. tropicalis show similar oligomerization properties and apparent affinities as C. elegans SAS-5CC-L.
claims.source: To investigate the stability of the coiled-coil domain across nematode evolution, we expressed constructs corresponding to SAS-5CC-L from Caenorhabditis brenneri, Caenorhabditis briggsae, Caenorhabditis remanei, Caenorhabditis sinica and Caenorhabditis tropicalis. In all cases, SEC-MALS analysis showed similar oligomerization properties and apparent affinities as for C. elegans SAS-5CC-L (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental SEC-MALS data from multiple species.

claims.claim: The trimeric coiled coil is an evolutionary conserved feature of nematode SAS-5 proteins.
claims.source: Taken together, these data suggest that the trimeric coiled coil is an evolutionary conserved feature of nematode SAS-5 proteins.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of structure and function across nematode species.

claims.claim: The Implico domain is a novel dimerization interface with no known homologs outside SAS-5 proteins.
claims.source: Structural and biophysical analysis suggests that SAS-5 can form tight dimers through its Implico domain, a novel dimerization interface with no known homologs outside SAS-5 proteins (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis and database searches.

claims.claim: SAS-5Imp forms a stable dimer as shown by SEC-MALS experiments.
claims.source: We found that this newly recognized domain is highly conserved amongst Caenorhabditis species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Importantly, SEC-MALS experiments revealed that SAS-5Imp forms a stable dimer (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental SEC-MALS data.

claims.claim: Crystals of SAS-5Imp diffracted to 1.0 Å resolution.
claims.source: Crystals of SAS-5Imp diffracted to 1.0 Å resolution and experimental phases were determined by SAD from mercury acetate derivatized samples (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is experimental data from X-ray crystallography.

claims.claim: The SAS-5Imp structure reveals a dimer composed of interlocked chains arranged in an antiparallel fashion.
claims.source: The SAS-5Imp structure revealed a dimer composed of interlocked chains arranged in an antiparallel fashion (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data.

claims.claim: Each SAS-5Imp chain features three α-helices (A1 to A3 and B1 to B3) that interact in a pairwise manner (A1–B3, A2–B2 and A3–B1).
claims.source: Each chain features three α-helices (A1 to A3 and B1 to B3) that interact in a pairwise manner (A1–B3, A2–B2 and A3–B1).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the crystallographic structure.

claims.claim: Proline residues at the linkers between helices in SAS-5Imp allow for tight 90° turns.
claims.source: Proline residues at the linkers between helices allow for tight 90° turns (Figure 3C), resulting in a very compact dimer of just ∼4 nm in diameter.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the crystallographic structure.

claims.claim: The SAS-5Imp dimer is very compact with a diameter of just ∼4 nm.
claims.source: Proline residues at the linkers between helices allow for tight 90° turns (Figure 3C), resulting in a very compact dimer of just ∼4 nm in diameter.
claims.evidence: This is measured from the crystallographic structure.

claims.claim: The SAS-5Imp dimer interface involves the majority of hydrophobic core residues (I219, I225, A229, L230, I232, I233, L237, F243, I247, V250, L251).
claims.source: The dimer interface (Figure 3D) involves the majority of hydrophobic core residues (I219, I225, A229, L230, I232, I233, L237, F243, I247, V250, L251); thus, breaking the dimer is expected to unfold the SAS-5Imp domain.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the crystallographic structure.

claims.claim: Breaking the SAS-5Imp dimer is expected to unfold the SAS-5Imp domain.
claims.source: The dimer interface (Figure 3D) involves the majority of hydrophobic core residues (I219, I225, A229, L230, I232, I233, L237, F243, I247, V250, L251); thus, breaking the dimer is expected to unfold the SAS-5Imp domain.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation that the dimer interface involves most hydrophobic core residues.

claims.claim: The high thermal stability of SAS-5Imp suggests formation of stable dimers even at very low protein concentrations.
claims.source: Given the high thermal stability of SAS-5Imp (Figure 1E), this suggests formation of stable dimers even at very low protein concentrations.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the high thermal stability and the structural observation that dimerization is required for folding.

claims.claim: The interlocked tight dimer structure of SAS-5Imp is a novel structural feature named Implico.
claims.source: This interlocked tight dimer is a novel structural feature that we named Implico, from Latin to entangle.
claims.evidence: This is based on the novelty of the structure as determined by structural analysis.

claims.claim: The two oligomerization domains of SAS-5 have the potential to drive formation of protein assemblies of higher-order than merely dimers or trimers.
claims.source: Together, the two oligomerization domains of SAS-5 have the potential to drive formation of protein assemblies of higher-order than merely dimers or trimers.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the presence of two independent oligomerization domains.

claims.claim: SAS-5 would readily dimerize even at low concentrations via the Implico domain, as oligomerization of this domain is tighter compared to that of the SAS-5 coiled coil.
claims.source: We envision that SAS-5 would readily dimerize even at low concentrations via the Implico domain, as oligomerization of this domain is tighter compared to that of the SAS-5 coiled coil.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of oligomerization affinities of the two domains.

claims.claim: SEC-MALS experiments on MsyB-tagged SAS-5FLEX revealed concentration-dependent oligomerization of SAS-5 from dimers to an approximately equimolar population of tetramers and hexamers.
claims.source: To test this possibility, we performed SEC-MALS experiments on MsyB-tagged SAS-5FLEX, which revealed concentration-dependent oligomerization of SAS-5 from dimers to an approximately equimolar population of tetramers and hexamers (Figure 4A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental SEC-MALS data.

claims.claim: MsyB-tagged SAS-52–265 shows analogous oligomerization results to SAS-5FLEX.
claims.source: Analogous results were obtained with a MsyB-tagged SAS-5 construct that lacks the disordered protein C-terminus (SAS-52–265) (Figure 4C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental SEC-MALS data.

claims.claim: Native mass-spectrometry of SAS-52–265 supports the presence of higher-order protein assemblies up to hexamers in solution.
claims.source: Moreover, native mass-spectrometry of SAS-52–265 also supported the presence of higher-order protein assemblies up to hexamers in solution (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental native mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: The SAS-5 coiled coil promotes the association of protein dimers towards higher-order assemblies.
claims.source: Taken together, these data support the notion that the SAS-5 coiled coil promotes the association of protein dimers towards higher-order assemblies.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing concentration-dependent oligomerization.

claims.claim: Earlier SEC-MALS analysis of MBP-tagged SAS-5 constructs of residues 1–260 showed formation of tetramers at an unspecified protein concentration.
claims.source: Furthermore, our results are consistent with an earlier SEC-MALS analysis of MBP-tagged SAS-5 constructs of residues 1–260, which showed formation of tetramers at an unspecified protein concentration (Shimanovskaya et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claims.claim: The SAS-5CC L141E mutant shows significant reduction of α-helical content in the coiled coil and a striking reduction in stability (Tm < 10°C).
claims.source: The CD spectra of the resulting SAS-5CC L141E mutant showed significant reduction of α-helical content in the coiled coil and a striking reduction in stability (Tm < 10°C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), whereas that of the SAS-5Imp I247E mutant showed absence of α-helical structure and complete loss of cooperativity upon thermal unfolding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental CD and thermal unfolding data.

claims.claim: The SAS-5Imp I247E mutant shows absence of α-helical structure and complete loss of cooperativity upon thermal unfolding.
claims.source: The CD spectra of the resulting SAS-5CC L141E mutant showed significant reduction of α-helical content in the coiled coil and a striking reduction in stability (Tm < 10°C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), whereas that of the SAS-5Imp I247E mutant showed absence of α-helical structure and complete loss of cooperativity upon thermal unfolding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental CD and thermal unfolding data.

claims.claim: The thermal unfolding profile of SAS-52–265 L141E shows a reduction in stability of the coiled coil by approximately 25°C, whereas stability of the Implico domain is not affected.
claims.source: We found that the thermal unfolding profile of a SAS-52–265 L141E mutant showed a reduction in stability of the coiled coil by approximately 25°C, whereas stability of the Implico domain was not affected (Figure 5A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental thermal unfolding data.

claims.claim: The SAS-52–265 L141E/M167E double mutant effectively abrogates coiled coil formation, with no effect on the Implico domain.
claims.source: Substituting an additional core hydrophobic residue of the coiled coil (SAS-52–265 L141E/M167E) effectively abrogated coiled coil formation, again with no effect on the Implico domain (Figure 5A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental thermal unfolding data.

claims.claim: Coiled coil disruptions in SAS-52–265 L141E or L141E/M167E mutants yield a stable dimer mediated by the Implico domain.
claims.source: As anticipated, coiled coil disruptions in either SAS-52–265 L141E or L141E/M167E mutants yielded a stable dimer in SEC-MALS experiments (Figure 5C,D), mediated by the Implico domain.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental SEC-MALS data.

claims.claim: The SAS-52–265 I247E mutant displays a single-step thermal unfolding profile with a Tm similar to that of the SAS-5 coiled coil in isolation.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found that a SAS-52–265 I247E mutant, where the Implico domain is disrupted, displayed a single-step thermal unfolding profile as measured by CD with a Tm similar to that of the SAS-5 coiled coil in isolation (compare Figure 5A,B to Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental thermal unfolding data.

claims.claim: SEC-MALS analysis of SAS-52–265 I247E shows a concentration-dependent trimerization, consistent with formation of just the SAS-5 coiled coil.
claims.source: SEC-MALS analysis of the same construct shows a concentration-dependent trimerization, again consistent with formation of just the SAS-5 coiled coil (Figure 5E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental SEC-MALS data.

claims.claim: The SAS-52–265 L141E/I247E double mutant shows no cooperativity upon thermal unfolding and remains monomeric in solution.
claims.source: Finally, a SAS-5 mutant where both oligomerization interfaces are disrupted, SAS-52–265 L141E/I247E, showed no cooperativity upon thermal unfolding (Figure 5A,B) and remained monomeric in solution (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental thermal unfolding and SEC-MALS data.

claims.claim: The two SAS-5 oligomerization domains self-associate independently from one another.
claims.source: Together, our results support the notion that the two SAS-5 oligomerization domains self-associate independently from one another, and that together they allow formation of higher-order SAS-5 assemblies.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the mutational analysis showing that disruption of one domain does not affect the other.

claims.claim: The two SAS-5 oligomerization domains together allow formation of higher-order SAS-5 assemblies.
claims.source: Together, our results support the notion that the two SAS-5 oligomerization domains self-associate independently from one another, and that together they allow formation of higher-order SAS-5 assemblies.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that both domains are required for higher-order assembly.

claims.claim: Expression of GFP-SAS-5 fully rescued the sas-5(RNAi) phenotype, allowing all analyzed embryos to progress to the 4-cell stage.
claims.source: Importantly, using time-lapse DIC microscopy to analyze the three transgenic lines generated in this study, we found that expression of GFP-SAS-5 fully rescued the sas-5(RNAi) phenotype, allowing all analyzed embryos to progress to the 4-cell stage (Figure 6C and Video 3), as in untreated wild-type embryos.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from time-lapse microscopy.

claims.claim: GFP-SAS-5 mutants that disrupt either the coiled coil (L141E) or the Implico oligomerization domain (I247E) were unable to rescue the sas-5(RNAi) phenotype.
claims.source: In stark contrast, GFP-SAS-5 mutants that disrupt either the coiled coil (L141E) or the Implico oligomerization domain (I247E) were unable to rescue the sas-5(RNAi) phenotype, such that all embryos underwent monopolar spindle assembly in each blastomere at the second cell cycle and thus failed to result in a 4-cell configuration (Figure 6D,E, and Videos 4, 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from time-lapse microscopy.

claims.claim: Both SAS-5 oligomerization interfaces are essential for SAS-5 function in vivo.
claims.source: We conclude that both SAS-5 oligomerization interfaces, and hence formation of SAS-5 assemblies larger than merely dimers or trimers, are essential for SAS-5 function in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the in vivo functional assays showing that disruption of either oligomerization domain prevents rescue.

claims.claim: Formation of SAS-5 assemblies larger than merely dimers or trimers is essential for SAS-5 function in vivo.
claims.source: We conclude that both SAS-5 oligomerization interfaces, and hence formation of SAS-5 assemblies larger than merely dimers or trimers, are essential for SAS-5 function in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the in vivo functional assays.

claims.claim: Only ∼30% of centrosomes in GFP-SAS-5 L141E embryos exhibited a clear GFP focus, with the remaining centrosomes exhibiting either no GFP focus, or only a weak focus.
claims.source: In the case of GFP-SAS-5 L141E, only ∼30% of centrosomes exhibited a clear GFP focus, with the remaining centrosomes exhibiting either no GFP focus, or only a weak focus (Figure 6G,I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: The vast majority of GFP-SAS-5 I247E embryos exhibited no detectable GFP focus at centrioles.
claims.source: In the case of GFP-SAS-5 I247E, the vast majority of embryos exhibited no detectable GFP focus at centrioles (Figure 6H,I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: SAS-5 oligomerization is important for centriole localization, with the Implico domain playing a particularly critical role.
claims.source: We conclude that SAS-5 oligomerization is important for centriole localization, with the Implico domain playing a particularly critical role in this respect.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the localization data showing that the I247E mutant has a more severe localization defect than the L141E mutant.

claims.claim: Formation of higher-order SAS-5 assemblies is essential for function even if centriolar localization has been achieved.
claims.source: Moreover, the presence of GFP-SAS-5 L141E at centrioles in one third of embryos, combined with the fact that this mutant completely failed to rescue the phenotype, raises the possibility that formation of higher-order SAS-5 assemblies is essential for function even if centriolar localization has been achieved.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the L141E mutant localizes to centrioles in some embryos but still fails to rescue function.

claims.claim: C. elegans SAS-5 lies at the heart of centriole duplication, given that it associates with SAS-6 and is required for SAS-6 centriolar localization.
claims.source: C. elegans SAS-5 lies at the heart of centriole duplication, given that it associates with SAS-6 (Leidel et al., 2005; Qiao et al., 2012; Hilbert et al., 2013; Lettman et al., 2013), a critical structural component for the establishment of the ninefold symmetry of centrioles (Kitagawa et al., 2011b; Van Breugel et al., 2011; Hilbert et al., 2013; Van Breugel et al., 2014), and it is required for SAS-6 centriolar localization.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Previous biophysical analysis of the SAS-5/SAS-6 interaction was performed using relatively short C-terminal SAS-5 peptides, as full-length SAS-5 proved difficult to purify.
claims.source: Previous biophysical analysis of the SAS-5/SAS-6 interaction was performed using relatively short C-terminal SAS-5 peptides (Qiao et al., 2012; Hilbert et al., 2013), as full-length SAS-5 proved difficult to purify.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: SAS-5 aggregates in vitro due to a ∼20 amino acid segment that may form a β-strand.
claims.source: Our results show that SAS-5 aggregates in vitro due to a ∼20 amino acid segment that may form a β-strand (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4); this site is outside the SAS-5 region implicated in SAS-6 binding (Qiao et al., 2012; Hilbert et al., 2013; Lettman et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations.

claims.claim: The aggregation-prone segment of SAS-5 is outside the SAS-5 region implicated in SAS-6 binding.
claims.source: Our results show that SAS-5 aggregates in vitro due to a ∼20 amino acid segment that may form a β-strand (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4); this site is outside the SAS-5 region implicated in SAS-6 binding (Qiao et al., 2012; Hilbert et al., 2013; Lettman et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of the aggregation-prone region with the known SAS-6 binding region.

claims.claim: In vivo SAS-5 may form a complex with a yet unidentified partner using the ∼20 amino acid segment, and this complex protects SAS-5 from aggregation in the cell.
claims.source: Rather, we postulate that in vivo SAS-5 forms a complex with a yet unidentified partner using the ∼20 amino acid segment identified here, and that this complex protects SAS-5 from aggregation in the cell.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain why SAS-5 does not aggregate in vivo despite the presence of an aggregation-prone segment.

claims.claim: Protein Phosphatase 2A binds SAS-5 in vivo and controls SAS-5 levels.
claims.source: It is intriguing to speculate whether Protein Phosphatase 2A, which binds SAS-5 in vivo and controls SAS-5 levels (Song et al., 2011; Kitagawa et al., 2011a), may interact with SAS-5 in this region.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: SAS-5 dimers cannot be disrupted even when diluting the protein to concentrations as low as 20 nM.
claims.source: Structural and biophysical analysis suggests that SAS-5 can form tight dimers through its Implico domain, a novel dimerization interface with no known homologs outside SAS-5 proteins (Figure 3). These dimers cannot be disrupted even when diluting the protein to concentrations as low as 20 nM (Figure 4A–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental SEC-MALS data.

claims.claim: The dimer mediated by the SAS-6 coiled coil is approximately 50-times weaker than the SAS-5 Implico dimer.
claims.source: By comparison, the dimer mediated by the SAS-6 coiled coil is approximately 50-times weaker (Kitagawa et al., 2011b), yet the human orthologue HsSAS-6 readily forms dimers in cells (Keller et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with data from cited studies.

claims.claim: The human SAS-6 orthologue HsSAS-6 readily forms dimers in cells.
claims.source: By comparison, the dimer mediated by the SAS-6 coiled coil is approximately 50-times weaker (Kitagawa et al., 2011b), yet the human orthologue HsSAS-6 readily forms dimers in cells (Keller et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claims.claim: It is reasonable to assume that SAS-5 forms dimers in the cytoplasm of C. elegans embryos.
claims.source: By extension, it appears reasonable to assume that SAS-5 forms dimers in the cytoplasm of C. elegans embryos.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with SAS-6 dimerization and the tight binding of the SAS-5 Implico domain.

claims.claim: SAS-5 dimers would associate with SAS-6 and possibly SAS-4.
claims.source: Such dimers would associate with SAS-6 (Delattre et al., 2004; Qiao et al., 2012; Hilbert et al., 2013; Lettman et al., 2013) and possibly SAS-4 (Cottee et al., 2013; Hatzopoulos et al., 2013), given the moderate interaction strengths of these associations.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from prior studies showing these interactions.

claims.claim: Formation of tight SAS-5 dimers through the Implico domain is necessary for SAS-5 localization to centrioles.
claims.source: Our work shows that formation of these tight SAS-5 dimers through the Implico domain is necessary for SAS-5 localization to centrioles (Figure 6H,I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that the I247E mutant fails to localize.

claims.claim: The SAS-5 localization mechanism either recognizes the Implico domain itself, or depends on a protein association that needs two copies of a distinct SAS-5 epitope.

results.result: SAS-5 contains two independently folded domains: a trimeric coiled coil (residues 125-180) and a novel α-helical domain called Implico (residues 210-265), separated by a disordered linker. The segment between residues 125-265 encompasses all structured elements of SAS-5.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C51 provide converging evidence from CD spectroscopy, thermal unfolding, and sequence prediction that establish the two-domain architecture of SAS-5. The experimental data (CD spectra showing two-step melting, thermal stability measurements) are internally consistent and support the conclusion that residues 125-265 contain all structured elements.

results.result: The SAS-5 coiled coil forms a parallel trimeric structure with moderate stability (Kd ~3 μM). The trimer is stabilized by conserved hydrophobic core residues (W133, M137, L141, I144, I148, L159, M167, M171) and this trimeric architecture is evolutionarily conserved across Caenorhabditis species.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C60 combine crystallographic data, MD simulations, SEC-MALS analysis, and evolutionary conservation to establish the trimeric coiled coil structure. The convergence of structural, biophysical, and evolutionary evidence provides strong support for this result.

results.result: The Implico domain is a novel, structurally unique dimeric domain with no known homologs. It forms an interlocked antiparallel dimer with very high stability (Tm ~72°C), featuring three α-helices per chain connected by tight proline-mediated turns, resulting in a compact ~4 nm diameter structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C71 present high-resolution crystallographic data (1.0 Å), SEC-MALS analysis, and thermal stability measurements that comprehensively characterize the Implico domain structure. The novelty claim is supported by the lack of structural homologs and the unique interlocked architecture.

results.result: The two oligomerization domains of SAS-5 drive concentration-dependent formation of higher-order assemblies. SAS-5 forms dimers via the Implico domain at low concentrations, then assembles into tetramers and hexamers through the coiled coil domain at higher concentrations (1-10 μM).
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C78 are supported by SEC-MALS data showing concentration-dependent oligomerization and native mass spectrometry confirming hexamer formation. The data consistently show progression from dimers to tetramers to hexamers, supporting the hierarchical assembly model.

results.result: The two SAS-5 oligomerization domains (coiled coil and Implico) self-associate independently. Mutations disrupting one domain (L141E for coiled coil, I247E for Implico) specifically abolish that domain's oligomerization without affecting the other domain, and both domains are required for higher-order assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C88 present systematic mutational analysis with CD spectroscopy, thermal unfolding, and SEC-MALS data. The independent behavior of the two domains is clearly demonstrated by the selective effects of mutations, providing strong evidence for domain independence and their combined requirement for higher-order assembly.

results.result: Both SAS-5 oligomerization interfaces are essential for centriole duplication in vivo. Wild-type GFP-SAS-5 fully rescues the sas-5(RNAi) phenotype, but mutants disrupting either the coiled coil (L141E) or Implico domain (I247E) completely fail to rescue, indicating that higher-order SAS-5 assemblies are necessary for function.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 are supported by time-lapse DIC microscopy showing complete rescue with wild-type but complete failure with either mutant. The functional data directly demonstrate that both oligomerization domains are essential for in vivo function, strongly supporting the conclusion.

results.result: SAS-5 oligomerization is important for centriole localization, with the Implico domain playing a particularly critical role. The I247E mutant shows almost complete loss of centriolar localization, while the L141E mutant shows partial localization (~30% of centrosomes).
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 and C109 are supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data showing differential localization defects for the two mutants. The data clearly demonstrate that the Implico domain is more critical for localization than the coiled coil, supporting the conclusion.

results.result: Formation of higher-order SAS-5 assemblies is necessary for function beyond localization. The L141E mutant localizes to centrioles in ~1/3 of embryos but still completely fails to rescue centriole duplication, suggesting that higher-order assemblies have a structural or organizational role independent of localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C97, C120-C122 are supported by the observation that the L141E mutant can localize but cannot rescue function. This dissociation between localization and function provides strong evidence that higher-order assembly is required for a function beyond simply getting to the centriole.

results.result: SAS-5 aggregates in vitro due to a ~20 amino acid segment (residues 282-295) that may form a β-strand. The authors propose that in vivo, SAS-5 may form a complex with an unidentified partner using this segment to prevent aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 are supported by experimental data showing aggregation and its elimination upon removal of residues 282-295. However, C102 is purely speculative with no experimental evidence for the proposed protective complex. The in vivo relevance of this aggregation-prone segment remains unclear.

results.result: SAS-5 forms tight dimers through the Implico domain that cannot be disrupted even at 20 nM concentration. By comparison with SAS-6 dimerization, it is reasonable to assume SAS-5 forms dimers in vivo. The localization mechanism may recognize the Implico domain or depend on dimeric SAS-5, potentially benefiting from avidity effects in SAS-5/SAS-6 interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C108 are supported by SEC-MALS data and comparative analysis. Claims C110-C112 involve reasonable inferences about localization mechanisms and avidity effects based on the structural data and known biology, though direct experimental evidence for the avidity mechanism is lacking.

results.result: SAS-5 concentrates at centrioles and likely forms higher-order assemblies there, with hexamers being the most probable oligomeric state. Hexamers formed through sequential association of three dimers would be kinetically and entropically favored over open-ended chains.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 is supported by fluorescence microscopy data. Claim C115 is supported by SEC-MALS data. However, claims C114 and C116-C119 are largely speculative, based on thermodynamic reasoning rather than direct experimental evidence. The hexamer model is plausible but not definitively proven.

results.result: The authors propose a model where SAS-5 assemblies assist SAS-6 organization by providing multivalent attachment sites and/or a structural framework. SAS-5 hexamers could recruit up to six SAS-6 dimers, increasing local concentration to trigger SAS-6 oligomerization and providing structural guidance for the SAS-6 spiral.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C135 present a mechanistic model that is conceptually appealing and consistent with the data, but largely speculative. The model reconciles structural findings with functional requirements and FRAP data, but lacks direct experimental validation of the proposed mechanisms.

results.result: The SAS-5 oligomerization model is conceptually similar to proposals for vertebrate STIL and Drosophila Ana2, though specific structural features appear restricted to close homologs. SAS-5 may have co-evolved with SAS-6 to accommodate the spiral architecture. Recent work shows Ana2 and STIL also form higher-order oligomers essential for function.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C144 appropriately contextualize the findings within the broader field. The comparison with STIL/Ana2 is supported by citations, and the evolutionary speculation (C141) is reasonable given the structural divergence of C. elegans SAS-6. The note about concurrent work (C143-C144) provides important context.

results.result: The study addresses a knowledge gap regarding SAS-5 function in C. elegans centriole formation. While SAS-6 architecture and function are well understood, the mechanisms by which SAS-5 functions were unclear. The work reveals that SAS-5 contains two self-associating domains (trimeric coiled coil and dimeric Implico) necessary for higher-order oligomers, and disruption of either leads to centriole duplication failure.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 provide appropriate context and summarize the main findings. The background claims (C1-C5) accurately represent established knowledge and identify the gap. The main findings (C6-C8) are well-supported by the comprehensive structural, biophysical, and functional data presented throughout the manuscript.
